newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices steady as Iraq tension eases.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices steady as Iraq tension eases.

text.p: Crude oil prices rallied on Monday then fell back in the absence of significant developments in the Middle East which last week sent prices soaring to their highest levels since the Gulf War.
World marker crude Brent Blend from the North Sea closed at $22.59 a barrel up 5 cents having touched $22.73 during the day's trading.

Traders said the market was driven mainly by technical factors but they had predicted a downward correction as hostilities in northern Iraq abated. Prices corrected as dealers bought product to cover shorts just before the market closed.

"The whole picture is reasonably bullish, but it's so quiet at the moment people just want to see fresh news from the Gulf for further direction," said one broker. "It seems to want to hold reasonably steady, and last week's high is the objective."

Prices moved up a dollar last week after Iraqi troops moved into Iraqi Kurdistan in support of a Kurdish faction, drawing U.S. retaliatory attacks against targets in the mainly Shiite Moslem south of Iraq and prompting suspension of a U.N.-sponsored oil-for-food deal.
Iraq, whose crude oil exports have been under a U.N. embargo since it invaded Kuwait in August 1990, was to be allowed limited oil sales for six months to pay for food and medicines.
Some oil refineries, which had allowed their stocks to run low in anticipation of resumed Iraqi crude sales, had to cover requirements at higher prices fearing a supply crunch.
Last week's rally also coincided with renewed demand for gas oil (heating oil) as the industry stocks up for the northern hemisphere winter with its diesel and gas oil stocks very lean.
With gas oil prices so strong, refiners can get more out of a barrel of crude as they switch from producing lighter products like gasoline in the summer to heating oil and diesel in the winter.
